newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW - NCR chief says acquisition a possibility.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - NCR chief says acquisition a possibility.

text.p: NCR Corp, which in January spun off from AT&T Corp with $1.2 billion in cash and a hope to boost revenues, sees an acquisition as one possibility down the road, its top executive said.

NCR's chief executive officer Lars Nyberg told Reuters in a recent interview in Tokyo that NCR, which eked out a small profit in the last quarter of 1996 after years of losses, would need a "buffer" as it moves into the second stage of its strategy of matching computer industry growth rates.
"As we are getting into phase two (of our business strategy), it's appropriate for NCR to be cash rich," he said.
"But I won't exclude the possibility to take equity stakes or the possibility of acquiring a company...(if) that will enhance our solutions to our customers," Nyberg said.
He did not deny a possibility of buying back its own shares, but said there was no such plan for the time being.
NCR makes supermarket and retail checkout and scanning systems, automatic teller machines and huge business computer systems.

As a result of a restructuring plan implemented in September 1995, it pulled out of unprofitable, low-end mass personal computer areas and entry-level servers, which contributed to its turnaround in the last quarter of 1996.
NCR's biggest headaches at present are its high corporate tax rates and slow revenue growth, he said.
"We have clearly said we'll reach nine to 12 percent growth and want to reach the normative tax rates over the planned horizon, two to three years," Nyberg said.
NCR in January said that its profits are weighed down by a whopping 75 percent tax rate.
"We have lots of plans to solve the problem of high tax rates and are actually determined to get the rate down to a more normal level," Nyberg said. "But it's a very complex issue."
He did not give details of the plans, but added a high concentration of its corporate functions in the United States was one of many complex factors affecting its tax rate.
On the revenue front, NCR aims to achieve 20 to 30 percent growth in its core business -- high-end computer systems for data warehousing and high-availability transaction processing, Nyberg said.
NCR also plans to focus on high-growth Asia and other emerging markets, such as Brazil and Russia, he said.
